data.title: Moral Evil, Natural Evil, and Free Will
data.sourcePassage: Philosophers and religious thinkers distinguish between two types of evil. Moral evil is suffering caused by human choices — such as war, cruelty, theft, and injustice. Natural evil is suffering caused by natural processes without human cause, such as earthquakes, floods, and disease. This distinction matters because religious believers who argue that God allows moral evil often appeal to free will: if God made humans free, they will sometimes choose evil. Genuine love and goodness require freedom. However, natural evil is harder to explain using this argument, since no one chose to cause a tsunami. The problem of evil is a philosophical challenge: if God is all-powerful and all-loving, why does evil and suffering exist? Attempts to answer this question are called theodicies. One well-known response is the soul-making theodicy: the world is a place where humans develop morally and spiritually through facing challenges, and suffering — while painful — may enable growth that would not otherwise occur.

data.title: Religious Responses to Suffering
data.sourcePassage: Different religious traditions offer thoughtful responses to the reality of suffering. Christianity teaches that Jesus himself suffered on the cross, meaning God is not distant from human pain. Christians find meaning in suffering through hope of resurrection and the belief that God can bring good out of difficult situations. Islam teaches sabr — patient endurance — and trust in God's plan, while also emphasising the importance of helping others in their suffering. Buddhism takes a different approach: rather than asking why God allows suffering, the Buddha taught that suffering (dukkha) is caused by craving and attachment, and the Eightfold Path is the way out of it. Hinduism connects suffering to karma and samsara — the cycle of actions and rebirth — while pointing to moksha (liberation) as the ultimate hope. Sikhism emphasises accepting God's will (hukam) and responding through sewa (service) to those who suffer. Non-religious perspectives argue that humans are responsible for reducing suffering through empathy, science, medicine, and justice — there is no divine plan, but there is human capacity for good.

topics: Good and Evil: Justice and Forgiveness

data.title: Justice, Forgiveness, and Restorative Justice
data.sourcePassage: When someone does wrong, society must decide how to respond. Justice requires that harm is named and that consequences follow — wrongdoers must be held accountable and victims must be protected. Punishment is one tool of justice, but it is not the only one. Christianity places exceptional emphasis on forgiveness: the Lord's Prayer asks God to forgive us 'as we forgive those who sin against us.' The parable of the Prodigal Son shows a father running to meet his returning, wasteful son and celebrating — not punishing — his return. However, Christian forgiveness does not mean pretending harm did not happen: it is about the victim being free from bitterness, not about excusing wrongdoing. Islam holds justice and mercy in balance: justice (adl) is one of God's key attributes, but every chapter of the Qur'an opens with 'The Most Gracious, Most Merciful.' Restorative justice is a modern approach where the offender meets the person they harmed and works to repair the damage. Rather than focusing purely on punishment, it seeks genuine repair and — where possible — reconciliation. Many religious and non-religious thinkers support it as a way of holding both justice and compassion together.
